notes: Interlocutory libel ruling on Chase tier meanings, justification particulars and Reynolds privilege; Eady J's reasons are detailed.

enrichment.short_title: Armstrong v Sunday Times: libel meaning and strike-out of Lance Armstrong doping allegations
key_facts: Lance Armstrong sued The Sunday Times and David Walsh over a June 2004 article linked to the book LA Confidentiel, alleging performance-enhancing drug use in cycling.
Eady J had ruled the article was capable only of imputing guilt or reasonable grounds to suspect Armstrong of taking such drugs, excluding the lowest Chase tier meaning.

The defendants sought to justify a third-tier meaning that there were questions warranting investigation; Armstrong applied to strike out superfluous particulars of justification and the Reynolds qualified privilege defence.
The defence pleaded 102 paragraphs of particulars spanning decades of cycling doping history, much of which Eady J held irrelevant to reasonable grounds to suspect this claimant.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Interlocutory applications in the Queen's Bench Division to delimit libel meanings, strike out particulars of justification and qualified privilege, and for security for costs and a prospective costs cap.
enrichment.outcome: Third-tier Chase meaning struck out; most historical particulars of justification disallowed; Reynolds qualified privilege defence struck out; £10,000 set-off allowed for US enforcement costs; no prospective costs-capping order.
enrichment.ratio: Where a libel is capable only of imputing guilt or reasonable grounds to suspect, a defendant cannot justify a lower-tier meaning that merely raises questions for investigation; repetitive 'questions' formulae and the repetition rule prevent evasion of the burden to prove underlying defamatory imputations, and Reynolds privilege requires responsible journalism including adequate opportunity for the claimant to respond to serious allegations.
legal_issues: Whether the Sunday Times article was capable of bearing a third-tier Chase meaning
Which particulars of justification were relevant to reasonable grounds to suspect Armstrong of doping
Whether the Reynolds criteria for qualified privilege were satisfied
Whether security for costs and a Musa King-style costs-capping order were appropriate

Jameel v The Wall Street Journal Europe [2003] EWCA Civ 1694
Lewis v Daily Telegraph Ltd [1964] AC 234
Reynolds v Times Newspapers Ltd [2001] 2 AC 127
Musa King v Telegraph Group Ltd [2004] EMLR 23

enrichment.short_title: Hall and Carter v Wandsworth: homelessness review and regulation 8(2) advance notice

statutes_considered.title: Allocation of Housing and Homelessness (Review Procedures) Regulations 1999

key_facts: Two Wandsworth homeless applicants challenged review decisions that they lacked priority need under section 189(1)(c) as vulnerable through mental illness.
Mr Hall had a history of reactive depression and psychosis; fresh GP evidence during review led the reviewing officer to uphold refusal without giving advance notice under regulation 8(2).
Mrs Carter had epilepsy and depression; the reviewing officer's letter inadequately explained why he rejected her GP's view of vulnerability.
Both cases turned on whether the original decisions were 'deficient' triggering regulation 8(2) and whether medical adviser opinions required prior disclosure.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Consolidated appeals to the Court of Appeal from county court decisions on homelessness review decisions under section 202 of the 1996 Act.
enrichment.outcome: Appeals allowed; both cases remitted to the council for reconsideration.
enrichment.ratio: Regulation 8(2) applies whenever a reviewing officer considers an important aspect of the case was not adequately addressed in the original decision and he is minded to confirm an adverse outcome; the Pereira test focuses on risk of injury or detriment when homeless, not ability to secure accommodation, and new medical adviser reasoning relied on at review must be disclosed in advance.
legal_issues: The meaning of 'deficiency or irregularity' under regulation 8(2)
Whether the original decisions applied the Pereira vulnerability test correctly
Whether applicants must be given advance notice of independent medical adviser opinions
Admissibility of a reviewing officer's witness statement to elucidate decision reasons

Runa Begum v Tower Hamlets LBC [2003] 2 AC 430
R v Westminster City Council ex p Ermakov [1996] 2 All ER 302

enrichment.short_title: McFarlane: permission to appeal EAT extension after employment tribunal strike-out
key_facts: Ms McFarlane's employment tribunal claim was struck out on 31 March 2004 after she withdrew from giving evidence when an adjournment was refused.
Her notice of appeal to the Employment Appeal Tribunal was two days out of time and the Registrar and HH Judge McMullen refused an extension.
A letter of 26 February 2004 from her representatives to the EAT, before strike-out, notified an immediate wish to appeal and sought an audio tape of the hearing.
On renewed application, Wall LJ held the letter might constitute a timely bare notice of appeal with later grounds following.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed application to the Court of Appeal for permission to appeal an EAT refusal to extend time for appealing a tribunal strike-out order.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal granted; appeal to be heard on its merits.
enrichment.ratio: Where an EAT appeal is marginally out of time, a pre-strike-out letter notifying an immediate wish to appeal and seeking materials to formulate grounds may arguably constitute a timely notice with grounds following later, warranting permission to argue that point on a full appeal.
legal_issues: Whether a February 2004 letter to the EAT amounted to a valid in-time notice of appeal
Whether time should be extended given distress and delay in obtaining representative assistance
Whether a struck-out claimant should be denied any appeal on the strike-out

notes: Major judicial review of Bluestone planning permission; lengthy judgment on section 54A and apparent bias is complete.

enrichment.short_title: Bluestone Holiday Village: judicial review of National Park planning permission

statutes_considered.title: National Parks and Access to the Countryside Act 1949
Town and Country Planning (Environmental Impact Assessment) (England and Wales) Regulations 1999

key_facts: Pembrokeshire Coast National Park Authority granted outline permission for the Bluestone Holiday Village, a large leisure development on the Park boundary near Oakwood theme park.
Council for National Parks challenged the decision for alleged breach of section 54A and apparent bias by county councillor members who had supported related County Council loans and permissions.
Officers recommended refusal as contrary to major development policy GE4 requiring overriding national need; members approved citing Pembrokeshire employment benefits.
Jack J held the authority properly weighed material considerations and that dual membership did not show closed minds.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of a National Park Authority resolution and grant of outline planning permission for a major development within a National Park.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; planning permission upheld on both section 54A and apparent bias grounds.
enrichment.ratio: Local economic benefits may remain material considerations under section 54A even where a development plan policy such as GE4 treats national need as unmet; apparent bias requires a real possibility of closed minds, and county councillors on a Park Authority may lawfully weigh planning merits differently inside and outside the Park provided they do not predetermine the decision.
legal_issues: Whether the Park Authority followed a lawful section 54A decision-making process
Whether local economic benefit could outweigh GE4's national need criterion
Whether county councillor members were apparently biased through loan and related permission support
Whether post-decision reasons complied with EIA regulations

notes: Leading three-dimensional trade mark appeal on cheese shape; Jacob LJ's ECJ-guided analysis is complete.

enrichment.short_title: Bongrain cheese shape: registrability of three-dimensional trade marks

statutes_considered.title: First Council Directive 89/104/EEC (approximation of trade mark laws)

key_facts: Bongrain SA applied to register as a series mark the three-dimensional shape of a segmented wheel of cheese, with or without a ridged surface.
The Hearing Officer and Pumfrey J refused registration for lack of distinctive character under Article 3(1)(b), despite Bongrain's evidence of use of a similar eight-segment shape.
The Court of Appeal awaited ECJ guidance in Linde, Henkel and Mag Instrument before hearing the appeal.
Jacob LJ held an unusual or memorable cheese shape does not automatically indicate trade origin to average consumers.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal from a Chancery Division judgment upholding refusal of trade mark registration.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; shape mark refused registration.
enrichment.ratio: The legal test for distinctive character is the same for three-dimensional product shapes as for word marks, but consumers are less likely to treat bare product shapes as badges of origin; a striking departure from sector norms is not ipso facto registrable without proof the public relies on the shape as a guarantee of origin, though acquired distinctiveness under Article 3(3) remains possible.
legal_issues: Whether an inherently unusual cheese shape possesses distinctive character under Article 3(1)(b)
Application of ECJ authorities Linde, Henkel and Mag Instrument to shape marks
Whether Bongrain's use evidence proved acquired distinctiveness under Article 3(3)
Overlap between Article 3(1)(b) and descriptive or functional objections

enrichment.short_title: Gezer v SSHD: Article 3 challenge to NASS dispersal to racist harassment estate
key_facts: Turkish Kurdish asylum-seeker Mr Gezer and his family were dispersed by NASS to deck-access housing on Glasgow's Toryglen estate in September 2001.
They suffered sustained racial abuse and a knife attack; they fled to London and NASS initially insisted they return to Glasgow before withdrawing that requirement.
Gezer had psychiatric history including depression linked to past torture; Moses J below found Article 3 threshold crossed but no breach by NASS.
The Court of Appeal held NASS owed no special duty to enquire into estate conditions for this vulnerable applicant before offering section 95 accommodation he could refuse.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal from dismissal of judicial review of NASS dispersal decisions under the Immigration and Asylum Act 1999.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; no Article 3 violation found.
enrichment.ratio: Where Article 3 ill-treatment arises from third-party violence after voluntary acceptance of offered asylum support, the State's positive protection duty falls towards the discretionary end of the spectrum; NASS was not required to make special pre-dispersal enquiries for a mentally vulnerable applicant, and adequacy of protection is judged on what NASS knew and reasonable police safeguards at the time.
legal_issues: Whether dispersal to Toryglen deck-access flats breached Article 3 ECHR
The scope of NASS's duty to investigate racial harassment risks before placement
Whether mental vulnerability required bespoke accommodation selection under section 95
Negative versus positive obligations under Article 3 in asylum support cases

R (Bagdanavicius) v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2004] 1 WLR 1207

enrichment.short_title: Gurung v SSHD: Nepal police officer asylum claim remitted for flawed reasoning
key_facts: Nepalese police inspector Gurung claimed asylum after Maoist threats and assaults linked to his counter-terrorism arrests of senior Maoists.
Authorities relocated him several times but advised he go abroad when further threats followed his role in arrests in India.
The adjudicator accepted his account but held fear no longer well-founded after he ceased to be a police officer and given a fragile cease-fire.
Police headquarters wrote that individual protection could not be guaranteed in Nepal's volatile conditions.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal from the Immigration Appeal Tribunal dismissal of an asylum appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; case remitted to a differently constituted Immigration Appeal Tribunal.
enrichment.ratio: Where an adjudicator accepts past persecution but finds fear ceases on civilian return, he must assess whether persecutors would know the claimant left the police, weigh contemporaneous official warnings about ongoing threat, and explain how protection sufficiency aligns with accepted objective fear at departure.
legal_issues: Whether Gurung retained a well-founded fear after leaving the Nepalese police
Sufficiency of state protection for individually targeted security personnel
Weight to be given to police headquarters' letter on ongoing threat
Whether Maoists would know the appellant was no longer an active officer

enrichment.short_title: Mortgage Express v Mardner: mortgagee duty of care on associated-company sale
key_facts: Mortgage Express lent £108,120 on an interest-only residential mortgage to Mr Mardner in 1990; possession was taken in 1993 after defaults.
After three months on the market with one failed offer, the lender sold the property for £68,000 to an associated company.
HH Judge Cox dismissed the lender's claim for the shortfall; a joint expert report valued the property at £82,500.
The Court of Appeal found the lender failed to show reasonable steps to obtain the best price when selling to a linked purchaser.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal from a county court judgment rejecting a mortgagee's post-repossession debt claim.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part; lender entitled to difference between debt and £78,500 (after allowances) plus three years' interest at 7%.
enrichment.ratio: A mortgagee exercising power of sale must take reasonable care to obtain the best price reasonably obtainable; selling to an associated company requires proof of good faith and reasonable precautions, and failure to evidence marketing efforts or justify a price below a joint valuation shifts recoverable shortfall to the price that should have been achieved.
legal_issues: Whether Mortgage Express took reasonable steps before selling to an associated company
The evidential burden when sale price falls below a joint expert valuation
Appropriate quantum and interest where duty of care is breached
Allowances for delayed sale costs and further interest
linked_authorities: Michael v Miller [2004] EWCA Civ 282
Tse Kwong Lam v Wong Loon Giam [1983] 1 WLR 1349
Cuckmere Brick Co Ltd v Mutual Finance Ltd [1971] Ch 949

enrichment.short_title: London Oratory School: judicial review upholding admission interviews
key_facts: The London Oratory School, a heavily oversubscribed Roman Catholic voluntary aided school, retained parental interviews for September 2005 admissions despite the 2003 Admissions Code banning interviews.
Peterborough Primary School governors objected; the Schools Adjudicator upheld the objection and required deletion of interview provisions.
The school argued interviews were essential fairly to assess Catholic practice across a wide catchment and that priest references alone were unreliable.
Jackson J quashed the adjudicator's determination for failing to address the school's material case and for disproportionate rejection of interviews.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Urgent rolled-up judicial review by school governors and parents of a Schools Adjudicator decision on admission arrangements objections.
enrichment.outcome: Adjudicator's determination quashed; objection not remitted; school permitted to interview for the 2005 admission round; Article 2 Protocol 1 claim dismissed.
enrichment.ratio: A schools adjudicator must have regard to the admissions Code but is not bound slavishly; failing to address a school's evidenced case that interviews are necessary to apply religious oversubscription criteria fairly is a material error warranting quashing, and removing interviews solely for minor guidance-note flaws would be disproportionate.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicator failed to consider material arguments for retaining interviews
Proper application of 'have regard to' the School Admissions Code paragraph 3.16
Whether criticism of interview guidance justified banning all interviews
Whether Article 2 Protocol 1 conferred a right to admission at the Oratory School

enrichment.short_title: Skanska v Egger: no appeal against non-consequential quantum finding
key_facts: In large construction litigation HH Judge Wilcox held Egger liable for delayed interim payments and assessed quantum in a second judgment.
Egger sought permission to appeal two quantum figures and a comment that Egger caused late agreement of the final account.
Tuckey LJ granted permission on the quantum figures but refused permission on the lateness comment, which did not affect any order.
Egger renewed the application; Waller LJ held the Court of Appeal has no jurisdiction to appeal a mere finding with no order consequence.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed application to the Court of Appeal for permission to appeal a comment in a quantum judgment that did not form part of any order.
enrichment.outcome: Application for permission to appeal refused.
enrichment.ratio: The Court of Appeal's jurisdiction is over orders, not intermediate findings of fact that do not affect the relief granted; a judge may reconsider such a finding when it becomes relevant, for example on costs, without being bound by it as res judicata.
legal_issues: Whether an appeal lies against a finding on lateness of final account agreement absent any order based on it
Scope of Court of Appeal jurisdiction under CPR Part 52
Whether the finding would bind the judge on costs
